nameStory: This grass earned the name 'bison grass' because European bison loved to graze on it, and Polish vodka makers discovered that the grass gave their Żubrówka vodka a distinctive vanilla-like flavor. It's also called 'sweet grass' for its wonderful honey-vanilla scent, which comes from a natural compound called coumarin - the same stuff that makes vanilla beans smell so good!
description: Bison grass is a medium-height perennial grass that grows in loose clumps, reaching about 1-3 feet tall. What makes this grass special isn't just how it looks, but how it smells - crush a few blades and you'll be amazed by the sweet, vanilla-honey fragrance that fills the air. The grass has flat, ribbon-like leaves and produces small, unremarkable flower clusters in late spring to early summer. It's extremely rare in New England, with only a handful of documented locations.

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Crush the leaves between your fingers and smell - you'll get an unmistakable sweet, vanilla-honey fragrance that's unlike any other grass in New England

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Flat, ribbon-like blades that are smooth and glossy, typically 6-12 inches long with a bright green color that has a slight sheen

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, scattered clumps rather than dense mats, with individual stems arising from creeping underground rhizomes (root-like stems)

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, brownish-gold flower clusters that are pyramid-shaped and about 2-4 inches long, appearing in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch, not rough or scratchy like many other grasses

habitat: In New England, bison grass grows in moist to wet areas like marshes, wet meadows, and the edges of ponds or streams. It prefers full sun to partial shade and can tolerate both acidic and alkaline soils. You're most likely to find it in northern New England, particularly in areas that were historically connected to Canada's boreal regions.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge bright green in early spring, and the sweet fragrance becomes noticeable when leaves are crushed. Flower clusters begin forming in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in early summer with small brownish-gold seed heads. The vanilla scent is strongest during warm, humid days when oils are most concentrated.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn golden-yellow and the sweet scent remains detectable, though less intense. Seeds mature and disperse in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving only dried stems and seed heads. The plant survives underground via rhizomes, ready to sprout again in spring.

funFact: This grass is so sacred to many Indigenous peoples of North America that it's considered one of the four sacred medicines, traditionally braided and burned in ceremonies - and that amazing vanilla scent you smell is the same compound that Polish vodka makers use to flavor Żubrówka, one of the world's oldest flavored vodkas!
confusionNotes: Bison grass could be confused with other tall meadow grasses, but the vanilla-honey scent when crushed is completely unique - no other New England grass smells remotely like it. Remember: if it doesn't smell like vanilla cookies when you crush it, it's not bison grass!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with 'buffalo grass' - that's a completely different species found in the American West. Also, this grass contains coumarin, which gives it that wonderful scent but can be mildly toxic in large quantities, so it's meant for smelling and ceremonial use, not eating.
compareHints: Bison grass differs from its relative sweet vernal grass by being taller, having a more intense vanilla scent, and growing in wetter habitats. While sweet vernal grass is common in dry fields and roadsides, bison grass prefers marshes and wet meadows. Alpine sweetgrass grows only at high elevations, and northern sweetgrass has hairier leaves and stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sweet vernal grass is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it relatively easy to identify among the sweetgrasses.
Unlike its lowland relative sweet vernal grass which grows in fields and roadsides, alpine sweetgrass is restricted to high elevations and forms much smaller, more compact tufts.
Northern sweetgrass differs from its close relative sweet vernal grass by being taller and having a more intense sweet fragrance, plus it prefers wetter habitats.
